content: 1. This section provides detailed recommendations for infection-control measures aimed at preventing the transmission of Mycobacterium tuberculosis (M. tuberculosis) in high-risk environments, including healthcare facilities. 2. The infection-control model developed for healthcare settings remains the most effective approach and is discussed comprehensively. 3. The recommendations have been updated to include an assessment of institutional risk for tuberculosis (TB), categorizing risk into three levels: low, medium, and potential ongoing transmission, based on community and institutional experiences with TB. 4. It is recommended that the frequency of testing employees for latent TB infection (LTBI) should be determined by the institution's risk category. 5. Additional recommendations address the control of TB transmission in correctional facilities, homeless shelters, and other newly identified high-risk environments. 6. The section on research needs highlights gaps in knowledge and technological limitations that hinder current efforts to control and prevent TB. 7. Further research is required to develop evidence-based tools for optimal diagnosis, treatment, and prevention of TB. 8. Public health policy and research priorities should focus on enhancing TB control efforts both in the United States and globally, with contributions from academic professionals. 9. A section is dedicated to graded recommendations for TB control and prevention, providing detailed guidance for each area discussed in the report. 10. TB is almost exclusively transmitted via airborne routes. The infectious organisms are carried in droplet nuclei, which are expelled into the air when a person with pulmonary TB coughs, talks, sings, or sneezes. 11. Person-to-person transmission of M. tuberculosis depends on characteristics of the source case, the exposed individual, and the environment in which the exposure occurs. 12. The virulence of the infecting strain of M. tuberculosis may also influence the likelihood of transmission. 13. By the time individuals with pulmonary TB seek medical attention, 30–40% of their close personal contacts show evidence of LTBI. 14. The highest rates of infection among contacts occur following intense exposure to patients whose sputum smears are positive for acid-fast bacilli (AFB). 15. Patients with cavitary pulmonary TB are more likely to have AFB-positive sputum smears and, therefore, have a greater potential to transmit TB. 16. These patients also tend to cough more frequently, making the combination of cavitary disease, AFB smear positivity, and frequent coughing significant factors for infectivity. 17. Patients with AFB smear-negative TB can also transmit the disease, but their potential for transmission is lower than that of smear-positive patients. 18. Approximately 17% of TB transmission is attributed to patients with AFB smear-negative pulmonary TB. 19. A study of elderly nursing home residents found that individuals with initially positive tuberculin skin test results during periods of endemic TB exposure had a much lower risk of developing TB compared to those with initially negative skin test results. 20. This suggests that preexisting LTBI provides some protection against subsequent infection and progression to active disease. 21. Similarly, prior TB disease was once thought to confer protection against reinfection with a new strain of M. tuberculosis. 22. However, molecular typing of paired isolates from patients with recurrent TB episodes has shown that reinfection can occur in both immunocompetent and immunocompromised individuals. 23. Vaccination is a classic method of protecting individuals exposed to infectious diseases. 24. The Mycobacterium bovis Bacillus Calmette-Guérin (BCG) vaccine is widely used globally (though not in the United States) due to its proven efficacy in protecting infants and young children from meningeal and miliary TB. 25. The protective effect of BCG in infants and children is likely due to its ability to prevent progression of the primary infection when administered during early life stages. 26. Epidemiologic evidence suggests that BCG immunization does not prevent infection with M. tuberculosis upon exposure and has not significantly impacted the global epidemiology of TB. 27. A recent retrospective study found that BCG's protective efficacy can persist for 50–60 years, indicating that a single dose may have a long-lasting effect.
